newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria Forcados terminal revamp 75 pct ready - Shell.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria Forcados terminal revamp 75 pct ready - Shell.

text.p: Shell Nigeria said on Thursday that a major overhaul of its ageing Niger Delta Forcados crude export terminal was now three-quarters complete.

The $450 million upgrade is scheduled for commissioning in January 1998 after a 12-month delay in construction which eventually got underway in September 1994, project manager Mike Thomas told visiting reporters.
"We have got just over a year of construction left to go," he said.
Forcados pumps about 450,000 barrels per day (bpd), almost half of Shell's huge Nigerian operation and a quarter of Nigeria's total crude oil output.
Redevelopment of the existing 25-year-old terminal is designed to replace obsolete equipment, increase crude storage capacity and enhance reliability.
New dehydration systems will boost storage in the 10 600,000-barrel crude containers by up to 40 percent by separating water from oil before it reaches the tanks.
The terminal's main pipeline will have capacity to handle 1.8 million bpd of liquid including water.
Six of the 10 tanks so far have been refurbished and four tied into the new continuous dehydration system.
"We aim to modernise the terminal without interrupting production or export. We have been successful so far," Thomas said.
Greatest risk of an output disruption will come in January next year when work requires cutting into one of the major export pipelines.
"We'll schedule for between tanker liftings so it shouldn't affect production," said Thomas.

Shell is also nearing completion of the new 60,000 bpd South Forcados Tunu flow station. The facility will start handling 45,000 bpd from next month. Work on two more 60,000 bpd Forcados flow stations is planned at Ogbotobo starting next year and at Odon in 1998.
Installation on a gas compressor to boost output on the Forcados system's largest field, Yokri, will start next year.

Shell Western division general manager Steve Ollearearnshaw said new drilling and production techniques would maintain current 450,000 bpd Forcados output. But he said budget constraints were preventing the large scale expansion of remaining reserves of at least five billion barrels.
"We have been struggling and whether we increase or not depends on investment," he said.
"Despite the budget problems we have managed to keep production up by squeezing production out of existing wells. That can't go on forever," he added.
Shell's operations owned and funded 55 percent by NNPC was owed 11.28 billion naira and $26 million by the government by the end of September, Ollerearnshaw said.
Forcados drilling activity dropped to just four rigs in 1994 as a result of NNPC's payment arrears but six rigs are running now and a further two are set to start by the end of November.

Ollerearnshaw said improved community relations had significantly reduced disturbances across the Forcados region and output deferrals had fallen to less than 100 bpd so far this year from an average of 10,000 bpd in 1994 to 2,800 bpd in 1995.

"We've only had two community disturbances this year which have involved the loss of oil. The communities are not shutting us in anymore. Two years ago they were shutting us in fairly regularly. Shell has increased community assistance in the past two years and sits in a local parliament with community leaders," he said.
"Shell had a reputation as being technically good but somewhat arrogant," Ollerearnshaw said.
I think we have made a real effort in the past two years to get close to the community. Things are definitely improving."
